A great painting for its pavilion at the World's Fair.
The world will be watching.
And Picasso cannot find it.
For weeks he draws a painter and a model in a studio.
Pretty, quiet, pointless.
The canvas waits, nearly eight metres wide.
The fair is weeks away.
He has nothing to say.
Now picture a small town in the Basque hills.
It is Monday afternoon, market day.
Farmers have come in with cattle and carts.
The square is full.
Then the planes come.
They are German, the Condor Legion, sent by Hitler to help General Franco, with Italian planes beside them.
For hours they bomb the town.
Fighters chase people along the roads.
By night, Gernika is burning.
A British reporter walks through the ruins and writes what he saw.
His story crosses the world.
In Paris, Picasso opens the newspapers and sees the photographs.
Black, white and grey.
A town that is no longer there.
Five days after the bombing, he starts to draw.
He does not stop.
His studio is an attic on the Left Bank, with beams and a long, dark room.
The canvas is so tall he climbs a ladder and paints with long-handled brushes.
Beside him, with a camera, is Dora Maar.
She is a photographer, and she is his lover.
Week after week she photographs the canvas.
Figures arrive, move, vanish.
A raised fist appears in the middle, then disappears.
It is like watching someone think.
In about five weeks, it is finished.
So now, a question to hold.
Why did the most celebrated painter alive, with all the colours in the world, choose none of them?
Keep that question.
We will come back to it.
Now turn around and face it.
Look to the far left.
A bull stands calm, almost bored, its tail curling like smoke.
And under the bull, a woman throws back her head and screams at the sky.
Look at what she is holding.
A baby.
Its head has fallen back.
Its eyes are empty.
Her tongue is a blade.
Stay with her a moment.
Ask yourself whether you have ever seen grief drawn so simply.
A few lines.
No tears.
Just a mouth that will not close.
Now let your eyes fall to the floor of the painting.
A soldier lies there in pieces, like a smashed statue.
His hand still grips a broken sword.
Look very closely, just beside that hand.
A small flower is growing.
It is tiny.
You could walk past it for years.
Many people see it as the one sign of hope in the whole picture.
In the centre, the horse.
A spear has gone right through it.
Its mouth is open in a scream, its tongue another blade.
Its body is covered in little marks, like the columns of a newspaper.
Above it, a jagged eye of light, with an electric bulb inside.
Here is a reading you will hear in Madrid, and it is only a reading.
In Spanish, a light bulb is a bombilla.
A bomb is a bomba.
Some say Picasso hid the bombs inside the light.
He never said so.
He refused to explain his pictures.
To the right, a woman leans in through a window, pushing an oil lamp into the dark, as if to say, look.
Below her, another woman staggers forward.
And at the far right, a figure throws up both arms inside a burning house.
There is no door.
Now step back and see the whole wall at once.
Here is the answer to our question.
Picasso met this horror the way the world did.
In newsprint.
In grey photographs.
So he painted it like that, a front page as big as a house.
And look at what is not here.
No planes.
No uniforms.
No name of a town.
That is why it could later belong to every bombed city in the world.
Stand with it in silence for a moment.
Look back at that mother.
What would you want the world to see, if this were your town?
Stay where you are.
The next story is about where this painting went next, and it begins here.
That is stop seven.
Stop seven.
You are still on the second floor of the Sabatini building, room two hundred and five point ten, in front of Guernica.
If the rooms have changed, check the map or ask a guard.
Picture a scheduled flight from New York to Madrid, in September nineteen eighty-one.
More than three hundred passengers.
Trays, blankets, a long night over the Atlantic.
Nobody on board knows what is in the hold.
Not the passengers.
Not even the crew.
The plane lands.
And then the pilot speaks.
He tells them who has been travelling with them.
Guernica has come home.
To understand why that moment mattered so much, go back to where we left the painting, in Paris.
The world's fair opened.
And Guernica was no triumph.
Some on the painter's own side found it baffling.
They had hoped for a poster with a clear message.
Instead they got screaming horses and broken statues.
So the painting went on the road.
It toured Scandinavia and Britain, then crossed to America, raising money for Spanish refugees.
It was rolled, unrolled, rolled again.
Then the Republic lost the war.
General Franco ruled Spain.
And a world war began.
Guernica could not go home.
There was no home to go to.
It stayed in New York, at the Museum of Modern Art, for more than forty years.
Picasso made one condition, and he never moved from it.
The painting would go to Spain only when Spain was free again.
He did not live to see it.
Nor did Franco.
Two years after the painter died, the dictator died too.
Then came elections, a constitution, and finally, that flight.
Now for the story everyone in Madrid will tell you.
It is a legend.
During the war, in occupied Paris, a German officer is said to have come to Picasso's studio.
He saw a photograph of Guernica, and he asked, did you do this?
And Picasso said, no.
You did.
Nobody has ever found a record of it.
But people keep telling it, because it says exactly what they feel when they stand here.
In New York, one morning, a young man walked up to the canvas with a can of red spray paint.
His name was Tony Shafrazi.
He wrote three words across it.
Kill lies all.
He was protesting a massacre in Vietnam.
He was arrested on the spot.
For a moment, it looked as if Guernica was ruined.
But the paint had landed on a thick layer of varnish.
Restorers wiped it away.
Look at the canvas now.
There is no trace.
When it reached Madrid, it was hung behind bulletproof glass, with armed guards.
Only months before, soldiers had burst into the Spanish parliament, firing into the ceiling, trying to bring back military rule.
The country's democracy was very young.
And this painting had become its symbol.
People queued to see it.
A few years after it moved here, the glass came down.
Now it is just you and the paint.
What is it worth?
It has no price.
It will never be sold.
For comparison, another Picasso, Women of Algiers, sold at auction in New York for about one hundred and seventy-nine million dollars.
Few would call that the more important painting.
This one belongs to a country.
And it will not travel again.
Gernika has asked for it.
Basque leaders have asked, more than once.
The answer is always no.
All those years of rolling and shipping left their mark.
The museum says it is too fragile to move.
A woven copy of Guernica once hung at the United Nations in New York.
One day, before a speech there making the case for war in Iraq, it was hidden behind a blue curtain.
The official reason was the camera background.
Many people did not believe it.
Think about that.
Sixty-six years after Gernika, the picture was still too dangerous to stand behind.
Before you go, find Dora Maar's photographs on the walls here.
Look for the raised fist that Picasso painted out.
You can take photographs too, without flash, unless the signs now say otherwise.
Next door is the building where this story started, the pavilion of the Spanish Republic.
Look for room two hundred and five point nine, or ask a guard.
That is stop eight.

tracks.title: Stop 8. Sert and Lacasa: The Spanish Pavilion

segments.text: Stop eight.
You are on the second floor of the Sabatini building, in room two hundred and five point nine, next to Guernica.
If the rooms have changed, check the map or ask a guard.
Look for a small architectural model of a building.
Picture yourself in Paris, in the summer of nineteen thirty-seven.
You are walking along the Seine, through the World's Fair.
Two monsters face each other across your path.
The pavilion of Nazi Germany, a stone tower crowned with an eagle.
And the pavilion of the Soviet Union, topped by two giant steel figures, a worker and a farm woman, striding forward.
Then, nearby, something small.
Light.
Almost fragile.
Steel and glass and panels.
It belongs to a country at war.
The Spanish Republic has built a house to tell the world one thing.
Help us.
Find the model now.
Look at how open it is.
No grand staircase, no marble.
A ramp carried you up and through it, past giant photographs of schools, farms and soldiers.
It was built to argue, not to impress.
Picture the ground floor.
Guernica hangs there.
And in front of it, something moves.
Silver liquid slides down curved metal plates, slow and heavy.
It is not water.
It is mercury.
The American sculptor Alexander Calder made it.
The mercury came from Almadén, Spain's great mercury mine, and the town lay close to the front.
Imagine the fountain saying, look what we still hold, and look what they want to take.
It was beautiful.
It was also poisonous.
Today the original stands behind glass in Barcelona.
The museum here owns a model of it, and if it is on show, look for it.
Climb to the upper floor, and on the wall a giant peasant in a red cap raises a sickle.
Joan Miró painted him straight onto the panels, taller than three men.
He is a farmer in revolt.
When the fair closed, the pavilion was pulled down.
And the peasant vanished.
What happened to him?
There are only stories.
One version says the panels were taken down and shipped off to Spain, and lost somewhere on the way, in the chaos of a war being lost.
Nobody knows.
Only black and white photographs remain.
A great Miró may be lying in a crate somewhere still, or long since burned.
Now look for something of Miró's that did survive, a small poster in this room.
Help Spain, it says, in French.
A figure raises a fist far bigger than its head.
Miró meant it as a stamp.
One franc each, to raise money for the Republic.
Back at the entrance stood a strange, rough column, rising some twelve metres, like a plant reaching for light.
Its maker, Alberto Sánchez, had worked as a baker.
Its title is a sentence.
The Spanish people have a path that leads to a star.
It was lost too.
But a copy has been made, and it stands outside this museum.
Look up at it on your way out, and think of who made the first one.
Now find a painting here of a sky full of dark aeroplanes, and below them, women running, clutching children.
It is called Madrid nineteen thirty-seven, black planes.
It hung in the pavilion.
Gernika was not alone.
Madrid was bombed again and again.
Look at the mothers in it.
Then think back to the mother next door, with the dead child.
The same scream, painted twice in one building, that summer.
The fair ended.
The pavilion came down.
Within two years the Republic was gone.
What it left behind is in these two rooms.
A model, a poster, a few photographs.
And one painting that never stopped speaking.
This is the last stop in the collection.
When you are ready, make your way down to the ground floor.
Check the map if you need it.
Your final story begins on the way out.
One last story before you go.
It is about this museum, and something it lost.
Picture a warehouse on the edge of Madrid.
Somewhere inside, there should be four blocks of rusted steel.
Each one is about chest high.
Together they weigh thirty-eight tonnes.
You need a crane to move them.
The American sculptor Richard Serra made them for this museum when it first opened.
He set them on the floor in two pairs, like a quiet argument.
The title names two bombed places.
Guernica, and an American air raid on Libya that same year.
After the show, the steel went into storage, with a private company.
Years passed.
Then a new director ordered a count of everything the museum owned.
The company had gone bust years before.
The steel was gone.
Thirty-eight tonnes of art had vanished.
Where did it go?
Nobody knows.
The favourite guess is that someone sold it for scrap, and it was melted down.
That is only a guess, never proved.
It is still one of the strangest losses in the art world.
Serra agreed to make the work again, exactly the same.
But he and the museum signed a rule.
Only one may exist at a time.
There can never be two.
If you have time, the new version is listed in room one hundred and two.
Check the map.
As you leave, look up at the glass lift towers on the face of the old hospital.
Ride one if you can, and watch the city drop away.
If you pass through the newer red building, step into its courtyard.
A giant brushstroke stands there, by Roy Lichtenstein, a painter's swipe of paint, frozen solid and standing upright.
After Guernica, it feels like a joke about painting itself.
Let yourself smile.
You have followed a painting from a burning market town to a Paris attic, across an ocean, and home again.
Think of that mother, and the tiny flower by the soldier's hand.
And think of your own road, Monica.
Amsterdam, then Lisbon, then the courts and fountains of the Alhambra, and now Madrid.
Thank you for walking with me all the way.
Enjoy Madrid.
